sec.title: Purpose
sec.p: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) is expressed in several solid tumours, including brain metastases (BMs) from lung cancer. We investigated quantitative [18F]PSMA-1007 uptake and treatment response in BMs of patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).

sec.title: Procedures
sec.p: Eleven patients with BM of NSCLC underwent 95-min dual-time-point dynamic [18F]PSMA-1007 PET/CT and a whole-body static scan before and after stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) with a median dose of 20 Gy (range: 8–25 Gy) given in a median of 1 fraction (range: 1–3). Seven patients completed both exams. Image-derived input functions were extracted from the internal carotid arteries, and pharmacokinetic analysis using Patlak modelling yielded the influx constant (Ki). Standardised uptake value (SUV), biological tumour volume (BTV) and tumour heterogeneity using the coefficient of variance (CoV) were assessed.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: [18F]PSMA-1007 PET showed uptake in the first exam in BMs and primary lung tumour in all patients. Significant inter-patient and intra-lesion heterogeneity in tracer uptake was observed in BMs with median Ki of 0.005 ml/ccm/min (range: 0.003–0.018 ml/ccm/min), SUVpeak of 4.2 g/ml (range: 0.4–34.4 g/ml), CoV of 0.36 (range 0.06–0.85) and BTV of 2.35 ml (range 0.03–22.29 ml). After SRS, reductions in Ki (37%), SUVpeak (50%), CoV (24%) and BTV (71%) were noted. Median SUVpeak in the lungs were 6.1 g/ml (range: 3.2–13.6 g/ml) at the initial exam and 6.3 g/ml (range: 3.8–11.8 g/ml) at the second exam.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: [18F]PSMA-1007 PET is a promising diagnostic tool for BMs from NSCLC. The uptake and heterogeneity, along with the marked reduction post-therapy, highlights its potential for monitoring treatment response.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is a leading cause of cancer-related deaths and frequently gives rise to brain metastases (BMs), with 15–20% of NSCLC patients presenting with BM at diagnosis and 40% developing BM over the course of their disease [1]. Patients receive various treatments, including surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, immunotherapy and molecular targeted therapy, alone or in combination. Targeted therapy has significantly improved outcomes in a proportion of patients with advanced NSCLC [2–4]. Further research is needed to better understand molecular targets, and Positron Emission Tomography (PET) provides a valuable tool for investigating these targets to improve treatment strategies and patient outcomes.

Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET imaging is an established method in prostate cancer imaging. While PSMA is primarily associated with prostate cancer, it is also expressed in other various solid tumours, including brain tumours, thyroid, breast, lung, colorectal and renal cell carcinoma [5, 6]. Histological studies have demonstrated vascular PSMA positivity in 48–85% of NSCLC specimens and tumour cell PSMA expression in 6–63%, with higher expression levels correlating with advanced stage or worse outcome [7–9]. Notably, it has been shown that PSMA is expressed not only in all types of lung carcinomas, but also in their BMs, reporting vascular PSMA positivity in 55% of cases and tumour cell positivity in 71% of cases [9].

To date, only a limited number of clinical studies have investigated PSMA-PET in lung cancer, and its biological and clinical relevance in BMs remains incompletely understood [10–12]. Early investigations have shown that PSMA-targeted tracers accumulate in both primary lung tumours and BMs, with uptake reflecting PSMA expression in tumour cells and neovasculature. These findings suggest that PSMA-PET may capture tumour angiogenesis and microenvironmental features that are not reflected by conventional metabolic imaging. However, the extent to which PSMA tracer uptake reflects target biology in BMs from NSCLC, and whether it has predictive value for treatment response, has not been systematically investigated.

The present study addresses this gap by using dynamic [18F]PSMA-1007 PET to quantify PSMA tracer binding in BMs from NSCLC. By applying full quantitative kinetic modelling rather than semi-quantitative measures such as standardized uptake values (SUVs), we aim to characterize the underlying physiological processes that drive tracer uptake and retention. Importantly, we also relate PSMA-PET findings to treatment outcomes following stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS).

sec.title: Patients
sec.p:
Eleven patients (median age 69 years; range 36–79; 5 male) were enrolled in a prospective, single-centre observational clinical trial (NCT03951142). The trial was approved by the National Research Ethics Committee and the Institutional Review Board (approval number 2017/1875). All patients provided written informed consent prior to participation. Eligible patients were those (I) aged ≥ 18 years and newly diagnosed with a new BM originating from NSCLC, (II) measured in at least one dimension as ≥ 5 mm on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted (ce-T1w) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and (III) eligible for radiotherapy and with a life expectancy of longer than 6 weeks. Recruitment occurred during routine clinical visits. All participants were referred for SRS as part of their treatment plan. Patient characteristics are presented in Table 1. Table 1

sec.title: PET/CT Acquisition and Image Reconstruction
sec.p: [18F]PSMA-1007 (2.5 MBq/kg) was injected intravenously, and the patients were scanned dynamically over the head using a dual-time-point (DTP) protocol at 0–30 min and 80–95 min post-injection. The exam concluded with a 2.5-min per bed full-body PET/CT scan. Scanning was performed on a Discovery MI PET/CT system (GE Healthcare, Milwaukee, WI, USA). The first exam occurred before SRS, and the second exam 12 weeks after the first exam. Notably, two patients (patients 1 and 4) underwent SRS two days prior to the first exam. The median injected activity of [18F]PSMA-1007 was 195.3 MBq (range 189.8—220.2 MBq) for the first exam and 197.9 MBq (range 195.0–219.1 MBq) for the second exam. Patients were positioned head-first supine with arms alongside their bodies. Brain PET images were reconstructed using Q.Clear (time-of-flight, point-spread function correction, 256 × 256 matrix, 30 cm field-of-view) with β-factor of 900, based on an in-house phantom study [13]. The whole-body PET data were reconstructed using the Q.Clear reconstruction algorithm with β-factor of 600. Dynamic PET data were reconstructed into 35 frames of variable durations (18 × 10 s, 6 × 30 s, 4 × 1 min and 7 × 5 min), and were corrected for radioactive decay, dead time, attenuation, randoms and scattering. A low-dose CT (120 kVp, 35 mA, revolution time 1, pitch 0.98, slice thickness 0.625) was used for attenuation correction. In addition, a diagnostic non-contrast-enhanced CT was acquired at the second time-point (120 kVp, 119 mA, revolution time 0.6, pitch 0.98, slice thickness 0.625).

sec.title: Image Processing and Analysis
sec.p: Image analysis was conducted using PMOD 4.0 (PMOD Technologies LLC, Zurich, Switzerland). To correct for patient motion, a rigid registration method was applied between frames. For the first time point, the reference image was the average uptake over the initial two minutes. For the second time point, the first five-minute frame served as the reference. A combined dynamic PET dataset covering 0–95 min post-injection was created by registering the CT images from the two time points using a rigid matching technique with normalized mutual information.

The BMs were segmented using a static image derived from the averaged uptake between 85- and 95-min post-injection. An individual segmentation threshold was determined based on the average signal from the blood background in the bilateral internal carotid arteries (ICAs). The threshold for each patient is shown in Table 2. The ICAs were segmented using a threshold of 50% of the maximum signal intensity from the early blood pool image (the first minute post-injection). The lung tumour was segmented using a threshold of 40% of the maximum signal within the tumour, based on previous [18F]FDG PET/CT studies [14]. SUVpeak and biological tumour volumes (BTV) were calculated for both the lung tumour and BM VOIs. SUVpeak was defined as the mean SUV of the five voxels with highest values within the VOI. Although SUVmax is frequently reported, SUVpeak was used in this work, as it better reflects the tracer uptake and is less sensitive to noise or single-pixel outliers. To assess the heterogeneity of tracer uptake, the coefficient of variance (CoV) was calculated by dividing the standard deviation by the mean SUV in the VOI. Table 2

The arterial input function (AIF) was approximated using an image-derived input function (IDIF) extracted using the time-activity curves (TACs) from the ICAs. Given that the ICA diameter (~ 5 mm) [15] approaches the spatial resolution limit of clinical PET systems, the IDIF is subject to partial-volume effects, leading to underestimation of the true activity concentration. Therefore, a recovery coefficient (RC) was applied. The RC was derived from an in-house phantom experiment performed under identical scanner, acquisition, framing and reconstruction conditions (including Q.Clear β-values) [13], and calculated as the ratio between measured and true activity concentration in vessel-equivalent structures. The resulting RC (0.59) was applied as a scaling factor to the IDIF, yielding an approximate 70% increase in arterial activity estimates.

Pharmacokinetic modelling was performed using linear Patlak graphical analysis to estimate the net influx rate constant (Ki) [16]. TACs were generated for the BMs using the average values in the segmented VOIs. A normalized time (t*) of 15 min was applied to ensure steady-state conditions. The Patlak model was selected due to the relatively slow pharmacokinetic profile of [18F]PSMA-1007 [17] observed in the 95-min acquisition window used in this study, which is consistent with prior findings in prostate cancer [18, 19]. The Patlak model provides a robust estimation of Ki in comparison to the microparameters obtained from traditional compartment models [20]. In particular, previous work has demonstrated that ICA-derived IDIFs in combination with the Patlak model provide a reliable estimation of Ki [21].

sec.title: Image Evaluation and Treatment Response Assessment
sec.p: A board-certified radiologist evaluated the response to SRS treatment using the Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology Brain metastases (RANO-BM) criteria [22] for the seven patients who underwent both scans, as well as the number of BMs from the radiological images. The RANO-BM criteria categorize treatment responses into four types: complete or partial response, stable disease or progression, based on (preferably) ce-T1w or contrast-enhanced CT. The MR exams were not acquired as part of our study protocol but rather obtained from clinical follow-up. The time interval between MRI and PET is presented in Table 1. For two patients, no MR images were available; therefore contrast-enhanced CT images were used as an alternative. One patient passed away shortly after the second [18F]PSMA-1007 scan and had no MRI or CT scan and was therefore not assessed with the RANO-BM criteria. For two of the patients an [18F]FDG PET examination of their primary lung tumour, taken as part of clinical routine practice within one month preceding their first [18F]PSMA-1007 exam, was compared to the [18F]PSMA-1007 scan by a nuclear medicine specialist.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Statistical analysis was performed with Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) version 30.0.0.0. (IBM Corporation, New York, USA). Normality of the data was tested with Kolmogorov–Smirnov Z-test for continuous variables. All data were reported as median and range. Correlation between CoV, SUVpeak and Ki were assessed using the Spearman correlation. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Patients and Treatment Response Assessment
sec.p: Seven of 11 patients completed both the initial and the three-month follow-up exams, while four patients deceased prior to study completion. As of August 2025, five of the 11 patients had died, with a median survival time after the initial [18F]PSMA-1007 PET/CT exam of 61 days (range: 37–136 days; Table 1). According to the RANO-BM criteria, one patient was classified as having a complete response, three patients as having stable disease, one patient as having partial response, and one patient as having progressive disease (Table 1).

sec.title: [18F]PSMA-1007 PET/CT in Brain Metastases
sec.p:
All 11 patients presented with uptake of [18F]PSMA-1007 in at least one BM on the initial PET/CT exam. A total of 23 BMs were identified on the initial ce-T1w MRI (Table 1), of which 19 showed [18F]PSMA-1007 uptake (Table 2). Notably, patient 10 had five BMs identified on ce-T1w MRI, but only one of these BMs showed low tracer uptake. Among the seven patients who completed the follow-up PET exam, eight BMs were identified on radiological images (two of these were not identified at the initial exam), and three of these were [18F]PSMA-1007 positive. Patient 1 exhibited [18F]PSMA-1007 uptake at both PET exams but had no second MRI exam. As shown in Table 2, all BMs with [18F]PSMA-1007 uptake in both PET exams demonstrated decreased SUVpeak, BTV, CoV and Ki in the second exam. Among the seven patients who underwent both PET exams, three exhibited no [18F]PSMA-1007 uptake at the second exam. After SRS, two of six patients had fewer lesions on the ce-T1w MRI examination, while one patient showed an increased number of lesions. All BMs that were contrast-negative on ce-T1w MRI images were also PET-negative in the second PET exam. A good correspondence between the [18F]PSMA-1007 PET signal and the ce-T1w MRI tumour region is demonstrated in Fig. 1.Fig. 1
Uptake of [18F]PSMA-1007 in patients 3 (a) and 10 (d) compared to MRI contrast-enhancing brain metastasis (b and e), and fused PET and MRI images (c and f). There is a strong co-localization of the PSMA-PET signal with the contrast-enhancing MRI tumour region. Patient 3 exhibited a high uptake of [18F]PSMA-1007 (a) while patient 10 exhibited a low uptake (d). SUV standardised uptake value

Figure 2 shows [18F]PSMA-1007 PET and MRI before and after SRS for patients 2 and 11. In both patients, there was a correspondence between the tracer uptake and the contrast-enhancing BM observed at the initial exam. After SRS, patient 2 demonstrated no uptake of [18F]PSMA-1007 (Fig. 2c), and hence no measurable disease. The corresponding MR image indicates that the contrast-enhancing BM had decreased in size from 8 to 5 mm in the longest diameter (Fig. 2b,d). Additionally, the follow-up MRI revealed two new smaller BMs, each with the longest diameter measuring 4 mm. These new lesions did not exhibit any [18F]PSMA-1007 uptake after SRS (not shown in the figure). Due to these MRI findings, patient 2 was classified as having “progressive disease” according to the RANO-BM criteria. Similarly, a good correspondence of [18F]PSMA-1007 uptake and contrast-enhancing region was observed in patient 11 at the first exam. In contrast to patient 2, the [18F]PSMA-1007 PET uptake remained detectable, although reduced, after SRS, while the diameter of the contrast-enhancing area on MRI increased from 18 to 20 mm. An MRI scan performed six months after the initial exam confirmed our suspicion that this was due to pseudoprogression.Fig. 2
Response to stereotactic radiosurgery as measured by PSMA-PET and MRI in patients 2 (a-d) and 11 (e–h). A strong co-localization between [18F]PSMA-1007 uptake and contrast-enhancing region was observed at the initial exam for both patients (a,b and e,f). After SRS, patient 2 exhibited no uptake of [18F]PSMA-1007 (c), while the BM was still visible in the MR image (d). [18F]PSMA-1007 uptake was reduced after SRS for patient 11 (g), while the BM was increased in size on the MR image (h). This later turned out to be due to pseudoprogression

The median SUVpeak was 4.2 g/ml (range: 0.4–34.4 g/ml) at the first exam and 3.9 g/l (range: 3.3–8.4 g/ml) after SRS (Fig. 3a), resulting in a median reduction of 50.5% (range: 37.3–58.0%). Notably, only four lesions showed uptake of the tracer at both exams. The Patlak graphical model produced excellent linear fits with a median R2 of 0.999 (range: 0.935–1.000). The median net influx rate constant, Ki, at the initial exam was 0.005 ml/ccm/min (range: 0.003–0.018 ml/ccm/min), which decreased to 0.004 ml/ccm/min (range: 0.003–0.005 ml/ccm/min) after SRS (Fig. 3b), giving a median reduction of 37.0% (range: 27.5–57.8%). Interestingly, a significant variation in [18F]PSMA-1007 uptake was observed between lesions and patients at the initial exam. The median BTV was 2.35 ml (range 0.03–22.29 ml) at the initial exam and 0.86 ml (range 0.72—2.21 ml) after SRS (Fig. 3c), giving a median reduction of 70.5% (range: 59.5–84.3%). There was a strong positive correlation between the BTV and SUVpeak (ρ = 0.90, p < 0.001) and between the BTV and Ki (ρ = 0.87, p < 0.001). A large variation in [18F]PSMA-1007 PET uptake was also noted within lesions, with a median CoV of 0.36 (range 0.06–0.85) at the first exam, declining to 0.29 (range 0.18–0.56) after SRS (Fig. 3d), giving a median reduction of 24.1% (range: 5.4–29.6%). Significant strong correlations were identified between semi-quantitative and quantitative tracer uptake measures (Ki vs. SUVpeak; ρ = 0.97, p < 0.001; Fig. 3e) and between the net influx rate constant Ki and heterogeneity of tracer uptake within lesions (Ki vs. CoV; ρ = 0.89, p < 0.001; Fig. 3f).Fig. 3

A large variation in SUVpeak (a), the net influx rate constant Ki (b), BTV (c) and CoV (d) was observed between lesions and patients at the initial exam. Among the patients who completed both exams, SRS resulted in a decrease in all imaging measures (a-d). A strong correlation was observed between semi-quantitative and quantitative uptake measures (e), and between Ki and the heterogeneity within lesions (f). The dotted line represents a linear fit. sec.title: [18F]PSMA-1007 PET/CT in Primary Lung Tumour
sec.p:
Of the 11 patients, two had undergone surgery and had no residual primary lung tumour. The remaining nine patients all exhibited [18F]PSMA-1007 uptake in their lung lesions at the initial exam. The median SUVpeak was 6.1 g/ml, with significant variability in uptake levels (range: 3.2–13.6 g/ml; Fig. 4a). Five of nine patients completed both exams, which yielded a median SUVpeak of 6.3 g/ml (range: 3.8–11.8 g/ml). There was a moderate positive correlation between SUVpeak in the lungs and in the BM (ρ = 0.65), but this correlation was not statistically significant (p = 0.067). In addition to [18F]PSMA-1007 uptake in BMs and the primary lung tumour, six patients demonstrated uptake of the tracer in metastases outside the brain (Table 2). Based on these [18F]PSMA-1007 findings, a case of prostate cancer was identified in addition to the NSCLC diagnosis in one patient.Fig. 4
[18F]PSMA-1007 and [18F]FDG PET/CT in primary lung tumour. a) A large variation in [18F]PSMA-1007 uptake (SUVpeak) was observed between patients, with SUVpeak increasing in three of the five patients who completed both exams. b, c) Comparison of [18F]PSMA-1007 and [18F]FDG uptake in two representative patients. Patient 10 displayed diffuse, moderate uptake of [18F]PSMA-1007 in the atelectatic left inferior pulmonary lobe and high, focal [18F]FDG uptake in tumour tissue, while patient 11 showed similar [18F]PSMA-1007 uptake compared to [18F]FDG. SUV Standardised uptake value

Figures 4b and 4c illustrate two patients who underwent [18F]FDG PET/CT examinations for their lung cancer diagnosis as part of clinical routine practice. The [18F]FDG PET/CT scans were conducted within one month before the first [18F]PSMA-1007 PET/CT exam and reflect metabolic activity in lung tumour tissue. Patient 10 exhibited a diffuse, moderate uptake of [18F]PSMA-1007, while the [18F]FDG PET images revealed intense focal spots (Fig. 4b). In contrast, patient 11 demonstrated a more similar uptake of [18F]PSMA-1007 in the lungs compared to the uptake of [18F]FDG (SUVpeak 7.7 g/ml vs 8.2 g/ml respectively) (Fig. 4c).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, we evaluated PSMA tracer binding in BMs originating from NSCLC using dynamic [18F]PSMA-1007 PET imaging. All patients showed uptake of [18F]-PSMA-1007 in at least one BM at the initial PET exam, and a decrease in uptake after SRS. However, significant variations in tracer uptake were observed between patients and within lesions, with one patient showing no uptake of tracer in 4 out of 5 BMs. These findings suggest that [18F]PSMA-1007 PET imaging is a promising diagnostic tool for investigating BMs from NSCLC and that the variation in uptake patterns could have implications for personalized treatment options.

To our knowledge, our study is the first to evaluate the dynamic uptake of [18F]PSMA-1007 in brain cancer and to assess how this uptake changes following SRS. While there are no directly comparable studies in the literature, Dias et al. reported a higher median Ki value than the present study in ten patients with prostate cancer imaged with [18F]PSMA-1007 [23], and that the level of PSMA expression can predict the prognosis of prostate cancer, with higher SUVmax values associated with greater tumour aggressiveness [24]. In BMs from NSCLC, Pei et al. reported an SUVmax range of 5.6 to 13.8 g/ml in six patients [10]. The higher SUV measures reported in our study may be attributed to imaging at a later time point (85 vs. 60 min post-injection) and the use of a different PSMA-targeting PET tracer with distinct binding properties ([18F]PSMA-1007 vs. [68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11). In two studies conducted by Pruis and colleagues using [68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11, they reported SUVmax of 4.0–10.7 g/ml at 90 min post-injection (n = 4) [11] and 5.0–12.4 g/ml at 240 min post-injection (n = 4) [12] in patients with BMs from NSCLC. The observed large variation in inter-patient and between lesions uptake in our study, differing from previously reported studies, may be attributed to a larger patient cohort or specific characteristics of the selected patient population.

Our results showed a wide range of CoV values, which could indicate significant variability in tumor biological behavior among patients. A study by Kurshid et al. [25] found that the higher heterogeneous PSMA expression in the tumour, the better the response to PSMA-targeted therapy. Although a wide range of CoV could predict patient prognosis and treatment response, a survival analysis was not feasible in our study due to the limited patient cohort.

The sizes of the BMs in our study varied significantly, potentially influencing uptake measures. Smaller lesions are prone to underestimating signal due to partial-volume effects, which may explain the lower SUVpeak observed for these lesions (< 0.125 ml) compared to larger BMs. Additionally, intra-lesion heterogeneity, as measured by CoV, was lower for smaller BMs compared to larger BMs. Although Patlak modelling produced excellent fits overall, the R2 values for smaller lesions were slightly lower (0.94–0.99) than those for larger BMs (> 0.98).

All nine patients with preserved lung tumour tissue exhibited uptake of [18F]PSMA-1007 during the first exam. Our findings align with those of Pei et al., who reported positive PSMA-PET results in all six patients with NSCLC, with SUVmax ranging from 1.8 to 5.6 g/ml [10]. Notably, like our findings for BMs, our patient cohort demonstrated greater inter-patient variability compared to Pei et al.’s results. We employed SUVpeak as the sole parameter for quantifying [18F]PSMA-1007 uptake in lung tumours due to challenges in accurately segmenting tumours and distinguishing between inflammatory and malignant tissue [26]. Only one patient (Patient 10) underwent systemic treatment between the two exams, leading to a decrease in SUVpeak, whereas the other four patients all exhibited an increase in SUVpeak.

PSMA-targeted radioligand therapy (PSMA-RLT) has emerged as a recognized treatment for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer [27–29], and PSMA-RLT is now being explored in other solid tumours [30]. Early case reports have indicated the potential applicability of PSMA-RLT in glioblastoma [31, 32]. However, challenges have been observed in other cancers, such as rapid tracer washout and low tumour dose in renal cell carcinoma and NSCLC [33, 34]. Larger studies are needed to establish the efficacy, dosimetry and clinical utility of PSMA-RLT in BMs. Notably, a higher pre-treatment SUVmean has been shown to predict better efficacy of PSMA-RLT in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer [27]. Given the large variation in tracer uptake observed between patients in our study, [18F]PSMA-1007 could potentially serve as a valuable tool for identifying patients with BMs for NSCLC who are eligible for PSMA-RLT. However, it is still unclear whether precise quantitative measurement of Ki is necessary for selecting patients for PSMA-RLT, and this requires further investigation.

Several study limitations should be noted. Firstly, absolute quantification of tracer kinetics requires a metabolite-corrected plasma function as an input function. The IDIFs extracted in our study represent radioactivity concentration in whole blood. Although Giesel et al. state that irreversible binding to blood cells can be safely excluded for [18F]PSMA-1007 [17], to our knowledge, no studies have investigated radiometabolites for this tracer. The lack of metabolite correction and a plasma input function could limit the biological interpretability of absolute Ki values. Secondly, the lack of histopathological confirmation means that some uptake patterns may reflect non-specific binding or unrelated physiological processes, particularly in the lungs. In addition, in BMs from NSCLC, PSMA is expressed both on tumour cells and in the lumen of tumour-associated neovasculature. Because [18F]PSMA-1007 does not cross an intact blood–brain barrier (BBB), uptake in tumour cells depends on BBB disruption, whereas vascular binding does not. Thus, the relative contribution of tumour versus vascular PSMA to the observed PET signal remains uncertain. Lastly, while most patients received their first PET exam prior to SRS, two patients were scanned two days post-SRS. This timing could potentially increase tracer uptake due to tissue damage in the target region. In addition, we acknowledge the limited number of patients included in this study, particularly the number of patients who completed both scans.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In conclusion, our findings indicate that [18F]PSMA-1007 PET/CT is a promising diagnostic tool for investigating BMs from NSCLC. The observed large variation in PSMA tracer uptake between patients warrants further investigation into the correlation between PSMA burden, prognosis and response to treatment. However, larger patient cohorts are necessary to validate these findings and fully explore the potential of PSMA-targeting therapies in NSCLC.
